newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - German centre helps Nazi victims win compensation.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - German centre helps Nazi victims win compensation.

text.p: Former concentration camp prisoners and slave labourers from the Nazi era are turning increasingly to a little-known small German town as they try to win compensation for their years of persecution.

The International Tracing Service (ITS) in Arolsen, central Germany, houses masses of valuable records from the Third Reich. The documents, ranging from cash books to death certificates, take up more than 22 km (14 miles) of bookshelf space.

The service was set up originally to help people trace loved ones in the immediate aftermath of World War Two. Now its main task is to help the Nazis' civilian victims or their relatives find proof of their persecution.

A flood of new inquiries following the collapse of communism and an increasing clamour from historians for access to ITS documents means these are busy but not always easy times for the service and its Swiss director Charles Biedermann.
"We're at an absolute crossroads," said Biedermann, who is employed by the International Committee of the Red Cross.
CHANGE OF ROLE
As early as 1943, the Allies began making plans for dealing with the huge wave of refugees and displaced persons they knew would be unleashed by the end of the war.

Renamed and relocated several times, their central tracing bureau arrived in Arolsen in 1946. The small town with a population of around 6,000 in rolling countryside 100 km (62 miles) south of Hanover may seem an odd choice for such a major operation.
But Arolsen had two main advantages -- its infrastructure had largely escaped war damage and it was close to the point where the British, U.S. and Soviet occupied zones converged.

In its early years, the ITS handled around 250,000 inquiries annually. Requests for information tailed off over the decades as people were reunited, lost hope or learned the tragic truth about the fate of their relatives or friends.
But with the end of the Cold War, the centre has taken on a vital new role.
Millions from the former Soviet Union or central and eastern Europe were able to write to Arolsen for the first time.

Under agreements which the newly united Germany drew up with its neighbours, many could also finally claim compensation or pension payments for the time they spent in concentration camps or as forced labourers in the Third Reich.

The number of inquiries -- which come from more than 50 countries -- has increased dramatically. Last year, the ITS received almost as many requests for information as it did immediately after the end of the war.
REINVENTING THE ALPHABET
At the heart of the ITS lies a huge index of 47 million cards. Workers check the requests for information against the entries in the index, which takes up three large rooms.
They have one major problem. "Often, the names are not written in their documents as the people themselves would write them," said Udo Jost, the head of the card index department.

A Polish prisoner could be asked for his name on arrival at a concentration camp, for example. The name would be written down by Nazi officials as they thought it should be spelt, which was unlikely to be the same as the Polish spelling.
If he had medical treatment, he might have been asked for his name again, perhaps by a Frenchman forced to work in a hospital. So his name would have another spelling on medical records.
To help find all the traces of one person, the ITS has reinvented the alphabet. The "alphabetic-phonetic system" enables workers to find all the references to one person.
In Arolsen, there are no double consonants, "j"s and "y"s count as "i"s and nothing begins with a "z".

If the index reveals the records someone is looking for, the request is forwarded to the appropriate departments. They then dig out the documents and provide copies or a certificate verifying the inquirer's claim.
BREAKING DOWN THE BACKLOG
The idea is fine in principle. But the ITS receives more than 200,000 inquiries a year. With only about 400 staff to deal with them, a backlog of around 300,000 remains unprocessed.
To combat the problem, the ITS has introduced a "fast-track" procedure where it quickly confirms that a person was in a concentration camp, for example, according to the card index.
The confirmation is accepted by many pension funds as sufficient proof to start payments to an applicant.
But the ITS does not give priority to compensation or pension claimants over applicants who simply want a record of their persecution during the Nazi era for personal reasons.
"Moral compensation can be just as valuable as material compensation," Biedermann said. "I don't want to play judge. I don't think I have the right to do that."
HISTORIAN OR HUMANITARIAN?

The Red Cross has run the ITS since 1955, although it is funded by the German government and overseen by an international committee. The service's mandate makes clear its role is primarily humanitarian and not to carry out historical research.

But some scholars feel the ITS's records are too precious to be closed to them and have lodged requests for access with the German government. The ITS has almost complete records from Dachau and Buchenwald concentration camps, for example.

Red Cross officials feel the humanitarian role must remain a priority and cannot be compromised by sharing the material with outside researchers. "Our main job is not to make things available to others. We're not an archive," Biedermann said.
"We're not against historical research but I don't think we're in a position to do it."
He sees scope for a compromise. "The solution we need is electronic data processing," he said.

The ITS has already computerised some of its operations and Biedermann suggests that if the entire card index were available on computer disk, scholars would be able to do their research while leaving the ITS free to concentrate on its humanitarian mandate.
